               BRIEF ON REMANDED ISSUE NOS. 11 & 13
            COMES NOW, Walter and Deborah McCullough, Dove Creek Ranch Partnership, Monk

Family Trust, Sherman Monk, Bar Lazy V Partnership, Dry Hole Interests, LLC, and NF5 Family

Limited Partnership (“Q11 and Q12 Intervenors”), and Cherokee Creek Partners, Bonnie Helene

McAnelly, Individually and as Trustee of the 2025 Homestead Trust and The Bonnie Helene

McAnelly 2023 Trust (“Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors”) and files their Brief on Remanded

Issue Nos. 11 & 13 pursuant to SOAH Order No. 35.

                                         I.       INTRODUCTION
           The ALJs correctly concluded that Applicants did not prove that Import Path 2 is necessary

for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public. 1 This brief addresses two

Preliminary Order issues that reinforce that conclusion and on which the record is now fully

developed. Issue 11 asks whether the proposed transmission facilities are necessary to meet state

or federal reliability standards. Issue 13 asks for the estimated congestion cost savings for

consumers that may result from the proposed facilities, considering both current and future

expected congestion levels and the ability of the facilities to reduce those congestion levels. 2

           On Issue 11, every reliability-standards analysis in the record was performed on the

Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”) as a whole, or on ERCOT’s statewide 765-kV plan.

ERCOT began each of those studies with all three 765-kV import paths already in the model. No

study removed Import Path 2 and asked whether any NERC or ERCOT reliability standard would

then be violated. ERCOT’s own PBRP found that a 345-kV plan with no 765-kV facilities at all

 also met every NERC and ERCOT reliability criterion. And ERCOT told the Commission in

December 2024 that only two of the three 765-kV import paths are needed by 2030.

            On Issue 13, the record contains no estimate of congestion cost savings attributable to

Import Path 2. Applicants nonetheless invoke congestion relief repeatedly as a benefit of the

project. The only dollar figures they offer compare one statewide plan to another, come from a

study ERCOT itself described as a qualitative comparison, and show the 765-kV plan producing

$136 million less consumer savings than the 345-kV plan in the nearer study year.

            Applicants classify Import Path 2 as a “reliability project” to avoid the economic tests,

including the congestion cost savings test. Having chosen that classification, they were required to

prove the reliability need for this project specifically. They did not.

      II.      JOINT APPLICANTS MUST PROVE NEED FOR IMPORT PATH 2 ITSELF

            Joint Applicants bear the burden to prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the

requested amendment to their certificates of convenience and necessity is necessary for the service,

accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public. 3 The Commission may grant a certificate

only on that finding.

            The PBRP’s approval does not supply that proof. The Commission’s own order approving

the PBRP requires each transmission service provider to “establish in the CCN proceeding that the

certificate meets all applicable legal requirements for a CCN, including the requirement set forth

in PURA § 37.056(a) that the certificate is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience,




3
    PURA § 37.056(a).

Q11 & Q12 Intervenors and Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors Brief on Remanded Issues
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-10397/PUC Docket No. 59182

Page 3
 or safety of the public.” 4 The Commission’s order assigning the PBRP projects says the same thing:

every project “remain[s] subject to the requirements under Chapter 37 of PURA.” 5

           The ALJs have already applied this principle. As the PFD explains, “HB 5066 does not

make a transmission project’s inclusion in a reliability plan a finding that the project is needed.” 6

Unlike the statute that governed the CREZ build-out, nothing exempts PBRP projects from the

factors in PURA § 37.056(c). 7 The ALJs therefore held that the Commission “must determine in

this CCN case whether Import Path 2 is independently necessary,” and that NERC contingencies

“are not a substitute for proving project-specific need for Import Path 2.” 8

           Preliminary Order Issues 11 and 13 must be answered against that same standard, that is to

say for Import Path 2, not the PBRP or ERCOT’s statewide 765-kV plan.

    III.      PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NO. 11 – ARE THE PROPOSED
              TRANSMISSION FACILITIES NECESSARY TO MEET STATE OR
              FEDERAL RELIABILITY STANDARDS?

           The PFD correctly finds that Applicants presented the project as one that will import power

into the Permian Basin, “not that the proposed transmission facilities are necessary to meet state

or federal reliability standards.” 9 The record supports that finding for four independent reasons.

              a. Reliability standards were applied only to the PBRP and ERCOT’s statewide
                 plan as a whole.

           Every reliability-standards analysis Applicants offered was performed on a plan, never on

this line. The foundation of Applicants’ case is the PBRP. ERCOT performed its reliability

Planning Criteria.” 10 ERCOT first identified local upgrades “with placeholder import paths

included,” and only then evaluated the import paths as a group. 11 For the 765-kV option, ERCOT

concluded that “[t]hree new 765-kV single-circuit import paths . . . are needed” to serve projected

2038 load. 12 Nowhere does the PBRP analyze the system with Import Path 2 removed.

         Applicants’ direct case adds nothing specific to this line. The Application restates the

PBRP’s methodology and conclusions, and Mr. Gurley’s direct testimony does the same. 13

         ERCOT’s later planning studies do not fill the gap, because they assumed the answer. The

765-kV plan in ERCOT’s 2024 Regional Transmission Plan used a start case that already

“incorporated . . . the three Permian Basin 765-kV import paths.” 14 The 2025 Regional

Transmission Plan likewise placed the full 765-kV plan in its 2030 and 2031 base cases. 15 A study

that assumes a facility exists cannot show that the facility is needed to meet a reliability standard.

         Applicants’ own witness confirmed that no one asked the project-specific question. Mr.

Gurley testified that he was not aware of “a study that isolated each line independently,” because

“they were studied together.” 16 No partial-build study was performed. 17 Staff did not supply the

missing analysis either. Staff’s need conclusion rests on the PBRP and the Application, and Staff

performed no independent need study. 18

Import Path 2 with a line rating of at least 7,602 MVA. 19 Applicants instead propose a conductor

rated at 7,131 MVA on the Oncor portion and 7,457 MVA on the LCRA TSC portion. 20 No witness

testified that ERCOT re-tested reliability performance at the as-filed rating.

             b. ERCOT found that every voltage options met NERC and ERCOT criteria, not
                just the 765-kV option.

         ERCOT’s PBRP comparison table answers “Meets ERCOT and NERC Reliability

Criteria” with “Yes” for the 345-kV, 500-kV, and 765-kV options alike. 21 A 345-kV plan with

five 345-kV import paths and no 765-kV facilities therefore satisfied the same standards. The

choice of three 765-kV paths, and of this 765-kV line, was a planning preference based on transfer

capability, losses, and cost. 22 It was not a requirement of any reliability standard.

             c. ERCOT did not find Important Path 2 necessary by 2030.

         The PBRP evaluated the 765-kV option for 2038 only. For 2030, ERCOT studied only a

345-kV option, which required two new 345-kV import paths. 23 ERCOT’s December 12, 2024

Sequencing Letter then told the Commission that “two of the three 765-kV import paths are needed

by 2030” and prioritized the northern and southern paths, not Import Path 2. 24 Staff’s April 2025

recommendation likewise reported that ERCOT gave all three 765-kV import paths a 2038

reliability need date. 25 Mr. Gurley conceded the 2038 date in ERCOT’s sequencing spreadsheet. 26

 The ALJs correctly found that the evidence does not establish that Import Path 2 is needed in

2030. 27

              d. Applicants’ reliability-standards arguments do not close the gap.

           TPL-001. Mr. Gurley suggested that the N-1 and N-1-1 requirements of NERC Reliability

Standard TPL-001 explain why the lines were studied together. By his own account, however, that

was an assumption: “So I assume, you know, that that leads into part of the recommendation for

multiple lines.” 28 He identified no TPL-001 requirement that would be violated if Import Path 2

were not built, and no study that tested that question. The ALJs correctly held that NERC

contingencies “are not a substitute for proving project-specific need for Import Path 2.” 29

           FAC-011-4 and the Far West Import Generic Transmission Constraints. Mr. Martin’s

rebuttal describes ERCOT’s Far West Import GTCs as interconnection reliability operating limits

under NERC Reliability Standard FAC-011-4. 30 That testimony does not establish a standards

violation that only Import Path 2 can cure. The GTCs are operating limits that ERCOT is observing

today, and they have produced no load shed. 31 ERCOT lists the 765-kV import paths, as a group,

as only one of seven upgrades expected to “help” exit the GTCs. 32 Mr. Martin did not author

ERCOT’s GTC study and did not run power flows, and no ERCOT witness testified. 33 Most

importantly, no study in the record removes Import Path 2 and shows that the GTCs could not

otherwise be managed or retired.

            All three by 2030. Mr. Martin’s statement that all three paths are needed by 2030 repeats

an April 2026 ERCOT presentation introduced on rebuttal. 34 It is a planning statement about a

package of projects, not a reliability-standards analysis of Import Path 2. It also conflicts with

ERCOT’s December 2024 statement that only two of the three paths are needed by 2030.

           The answer to Issue 11 on this record is therefore no. Applicants did not prove that Import

Path 2 is necessary to meet any state or federal reliability standard.

     IV.      PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NO. 13 – WHAT IS THE ESTIMATED
              CONGESTION COST SAVINGS FOR CONSUMERS THAT MY RESULT
              FROM THE PROPOSED TRANSMISSION FACILITIES CONDISERING
              BOTH CURRENT AND FUTURE EXPECTED CONGESTION LEVELS AND
              THE ABILITY OF THE POROPOSED TRANSMISSION FACILITIES TO
              REDUCE THOSE CONGESTION LEVELS?

           The PFD correctly finds that Applicants did not submit an estimate of congestion cost

savings to consumers and that “the record contains no evidence quantifying” them. 35 The full

record confirms that finding and shows why it matters.

              a. No witness or document estimates congestion savings for Import Path 2.

           The Application’s need and alternatives responses never use the word “congestion.” 36 That

omission was deliberate. Applicants disclaim any obligation to provide the estimate, asserting that

“reliability projects are expressly exempt from the economic tests, including the congestion cost

savings test.” 37

           The documents Applicants rely on are equally silent. The PBRP, Applicants’ central need

document, contains no economic, production cost, or congestion analysis of any kind. 38 ERCOT’s

Path 2 was not among the projects evaluated. 39

         Staff’s testimony does not supply an estimate. Mr. Poole recites Issue 13 but offers no

figure. 40 The most Staff said on the subject, in its 2025 recommendation on import path voltage,

is that shifting bulk transfer to 765-kV “may help reduce congestion on the lower voltage lines.” 41

             b. Applicants rely on congestion benefits they never quantified.

         Applicants cannot claim the benefit of congestion relief while declining to estimate it, yet

that is what their witnesses did. Mr. Gurley testified that the project crosses the West Texas Export

Interface and sits near the Hargrove to Twin Buttes and Bell County to Salado constraints, which

he described as “three of the costliest constraints” on the ERCOT system. 42 He answered “Yes” to

the question posed in his own direct testimony, “Are the congestion cost savings for ERCOT

customers significant?” and cited a market-monitor estimate of $10 billion in congestion costs

from 2020 to 2024. 43 That figure measures historical congestion across ERCOT. It says nothing

about how much congestion Import Path 2 would relieve.

         Mr. Gurley went further, testifying that a 765-kV backbone would provide “over $270

million in annual cost savings” compared with a 345-kV alternative. 44 No exhibit supports that

number. ERCOT’s comparison report shows $229 million in consumer energy cost savings and

$28 million in production cost savings, which together total $257 million, and production cost

             c. The only figures in the record are plan-level and do not answer the questions
                in Issue No. 13.

        The single quantitative source in the record, ERCOT’s comparison of its 345-kV and 765-

kV plans, cannot supply the missing estimate. 47 To begin with, it addresses the wrong subject. It

compares ERCOT’s entire statewide 765-kV plan to an entire 345-kV plan and does not isolate

Import Path 2. 48 ERCOT also described the exercise as an analysis performed “[t]o qualitatively

compare” the two plans, not to estimate savings from any one facility. 49

        The study’s assumptions are also out of step with Applicants’ own case. ERCOT’s

economic cases excluded the large loads supported by transmission service provider officer letters,

along with the reliability projects needed to serve them. 50 Those are the same loads on which

Applicants’ need case depends.

        The results, moreover, do not uniformly favor the 765-kV plan. In study year 2034, the

765-kV plan produced $136 million less system-wide consumer energy cost savings than the 345-

kV plan; only in 2039 did it produce $229 million more. 51 ERCOT itself cautioned that future

conditions may differ from the scenarios studied. 52 And even with the full 765-kV plan in place,

ERCOT’s 2025 Regional Transmission Plan projects West Texas Export congestion rent of $209

attributable to Import Path 2.

              d. The absence of evidence has consequences.

        The ALJs need not revisit Finding of Fact 225 to give the missing evidence its proper effect.

Because no congestion savings were quantified, none can be weighed in Applicants’ favor under

PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(E), which directs the Commission to consider “the probable improvement

of service or lowering of cost to consumers in the area.” 54 Mr. Gurley himself testified that

“lowering of cost to consumers” generally applies to economic projects, and that Import Path 2 is

not one. 55

        The absence of evidence matters for a second reason. Applicants avoid the congestion cost

savings test only by classifying Import Path 2 as a reliability project. That classification is not self-

proving. If Applicants have not proved that Import Path 2 is needed to meet any reliability standard,

they are left with neither showing: no project-specific reliability need, and no estimate of economic

benefit.

        The answer to Issue 13 on this record is that there is no estimate. Applicants offered no

evidence of current or future congestion levels that specifically Import Path 2 would reduce, or of

any resulting savings to consumers.

standards were applied to the PBRP and to ERCOT’s statewide plan, never specifically to Import
